entries.query_str: best headphones for mixing beats under 200, i mostly do hip hop in fl studio, 808s matter
entries.answer:
For mixing with a lot of sub-bass, you want **open-back or semi-open headphones with a reasonably flat low end**, and you want to know how they deviate so you can compensate [1][2]. Common picks in that range:

- **Open-back studio models around $150–200** (several brands make one): most neutral, best stereo image, but leak sound and have less sub-bass extension — you'll hear 808 *pitch* well but feel less of the sub [1].
- **Closed-back studio monitors around $100–170**: more isolation and more low end, often with a bass or treble bump; good for tracking and late-night work [2].
- **Pair any of them with a correction profile** (e.g., a headphone EQ plugin with a measured profile) to flatten the response — this matters more than the specific model [3].

For 808s specifically: check your low end on a spectrum analyzer and on a second system (car, earbuds), because no headphone under $200 reproduces 30–40 Hz reliably [3].

entries.query_str: is headphone correction actually worth it or a gimmick
entries.answer: It's worth it if you mix mostly on headphones. Correction can't add bass extension the driver doesn't have, but it removes the model's built-in tilts (e.g., a 6 dB treble peak) so your EQ decisions translate better to other systems [1][2]. Turn it **off when bouncing** — it should only be on your monitoring path, not the master.
